gloss: A small pit dug in the ground where a soldier can take cover.
examples: The soldiers spent the night in a muddy *foxhole*.
They dug *foxholes* along the ridge before dark.
There are no atheists in a *foxhole*, my grandfather used to say.

gloss: A shape whose small parts look like smaller copies of the whole shape.
examples: A snowflake is a natural *fractal*.
The screensaver draws colorful *fractals* that never repeat.
He wrote a program that zooms into a *fractal* forever.

gloss: The quality of being easily broken or easily harmed.
examples: The *fragility* of the old glass surprised everyone.
The crisis exposed the *fragility* of the banking system.
There is a certain *fragility* in her voice when she talks about it.

gloss: A small piece broken off from something larger.
examples: A *fragment* of the vase was still under the couch.
Archaeologists found *fragments* of pottery at the site.
I only caught a *fragment* of the conversation.
contrast: The noun is FRAG-muhnt; the verb *to fragment* is frag-MENT.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Weakness of body or health, or, in the plural, faults of character.
examples: Age and *frailty* finally forced him to give up driving.
The novel is honest about human *frailties*.
She loved him in spite of his *frailties*.

gloss: The unit of money used in Switzerland and several other countries.
examples: The hotel charged us two hundred *francs* a night.
The Swiss *franc* rose against the dollar this week.
He still has a few old *francs* in a drawer.
contrast: Sounds exactly like the adjective *frank* (honest).

gloss: The habit of saying what you really think, openly and directly.
examples: I appreciate your *frankness* about the risks.
She answered with a *frankness* that startled the reporters.
His *frankness* has cost him a few friends.

gloss: A social club for male students at an American college.
examples: He joined a *fraternity* his sophomore year.
Several *fraternities* were suspended after the incident.
The party was at the *fraternity* house on Elm Street.
contrast: Students shorten it to *frat*; the women's version is a *sorority*.

gloss: Someone obsessed with a particular thing, or someone who behaves very strangely.
examples: My brother is a total fitness *freak*.
Don't be a control *freak* about the seating chart.
The kids in the back row called him a *freak*.
contrast: Calling a person a *freak* is an insult; a fitness or control *freak* is teasing.

gloss: Someone who takes food, money, or favors from others without giving anything back.
examples: My cousin is a *freeloader* who never buys a round.
The landlord called them *freeloaders* and changed the locks.
He lived like a *freeloader* on his friends' couches for a year.

gloss: A race or event in which the competitor chooses the style, especially the front crawl in swimming.
examples: She swims *freestyle* better than backstroke.
He took gold in the 400-meter *freestyle*.
Coach has us doing *freestyle* for the first twenty minutes.

gloss: An official stop on rises in pay, prices, or hiring, or a spell of very cold weather.
examples: The company announced a hiring *freeze* in March.
A hard *freeze* is expected tonight, so cover the plants.
Two rent *freezes* in a row kept my apartment affordable.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *frees* (sets free).

gloss: A product that makes the air or your breath smell better.
examples: He hung a pine air *freshener* from the mirror.
The bathroom *freshener* ran out weeks ago.
They sell little *fresheners* shaped like trees at the car wash.

gloss: One of the metal bars across the neck of a guitar that mark where to press the strings.
examples: Put your finger just behind the third *fret*.
The *frets* on this old guitar are worn flat.
A bass usually has fewer *frets* than a guitar.

gloss: A member of a Catholic religious order who lives and works among ordinary people.
examples: A *friar* in a brown robe opened the door.
The *friars* ran a soup kitchen behind the church.
In the play, a *friar* secretly marries the young couple.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *fryer*, the kitchen appliance.

gloss: Kind and welcoming behavior toward other people.
examples: The *friendliness* of the staff made the trip.
There was a forced *friendliness* in his voice.
Small towns here are known for their *friendliness*.

gloss: A fast medium-sized warship used mainly to escort other ships.
examples: The navy sent a *frigate* to escort the convoy.
Two *frigates* are docked at the base this week.
The *frigate* was launched in 1998 and retired last year.

gloss: A gathered strip of cloth sewn along an edge as decoration.
examples: The dress has a lace *frill* at the hem.
She hates *frills* and bows on children's clothes.
A narrow *frill* runs around the edge of the pillow.
contrast: In the plural, *frills* also means unnecessary extras: a no-*frills* airline.

gloss: A thick Italian omelet cooked slowly with vegetables or cheese mixed in.
examples: I made a spinach *frittata* for brunch.
The cafe serves *frittatas* until noon.
Leftover potatoes go great in a *frittata*.

gloss: A piece of fruit, vegetable, or meat coated in batter and fried.
examples: The bakery's apple *fritter* is the size of my hand.
We ordered corn *fritters* as an appetizer.
She fried a *fritter* for each of the kids.

gloss: Behavior that is not serious, especially when seriousness is expected.
examples: There was no time for *frivolity* the week before the launch.
He dismissed the whole festival as expensive *frivolity*.
A little *frivolity* is good for morale.

gloss: The large divided leaf of a fern or palm.
examples: A palm *frond* had blown onto the driveway.
The fern's new *fronds* uncurl in the spring.
He fanned himself with a broad *frond*.

ru: граница освоенных земель; рубеж, передний край
gloss: The edge of settled land, or the edge of what is known in some field.
examples: Her family moved west when this was still the *frontier*.
Gene therapy is one of the *frontiers* of medicine.
The town grew up on the *frontier* in the 1870s.
contrast: Americans stress the second syllable, frun-TEER; the British stress the first.

gloss: The natural sugar found in fruit and honey.
examples: Soda is loaded with *fructose* from corn syrup.
Ripe pears are high in *fructose*.
Some people have trouble digesting *fructose*.

gloss: The habit of spending very little money.
examples: Her *frugality* got the family through the recession.
He talks about *frugality* but drives a new truck.
Years of *frugality* paid off when they bought the house.

gloss: A heavy cake full of dried fruit and nuts, traditionally eaten at Christmas.
examples: My aunt mails us a *fruitcake* every December.
Nobody at the party would touch the *fruitcake*.
He cut a thin slice of *fruitcake* to be polite.
contrast: Calling a person a *fruitcake* means they are crazy.

gloss: The point at which a plan or hope finally becomes real.
examples: The project came to *fruition* after six years.
He never saw his idea come to *fruition*.
Their plans reached *fruition* only last spring.
contrast: Said froo-IH-shuhn — the *fruit* spelling is misleading.

gloss: A machine or deep pan used for cooking food in hot oil or hot air.
examples: We got an air *fryer* for Christmas.
The restaurant's *fryers* are cleaned every night.
Drop the wings in the *fryer* for eight minutes.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *friar*, the monk.

gloss: A garden plant with hanging pink and purple flowers, or the bright pink color of those flowers.
examples: A *fuchsia* hung in a basket by the porch.
She wore a scarf in bright *fuchsia*.
The nursery sells *fuchsias* every spring.
contrast: Spelled f-u-c-h-s-i-a but said FYOO-shuh; the misspelling *fuschia* is everywhere.

gloss: A soft, rich candy made from sugar, butter, and milk.
examples: She brought a box of chocolate *fudge* to the office.
The shop on the boardwalk makes *fudge* right in the window.
One piece of *fudge* is enough for me.

gloss: A piece of music in which a short tune is introduced and then repeated by other voices in turn.
examples: She played a Bach *fugue* for the audition.
The organist ended with a thundering *fugue*.
His *fugues* are harder than they sound.
contrast: One syllable, FYOOG, with the *ue* silent.

gloss: The fixed point on which a lever turns.
examples: Move the *fulcrum* closer and the bar lifts more weight.
A seesaw's *fulcrum* is the bar under the middle.
Their star player is the *fulcrum* of the whole offense.

gloss: A player positioned toward the back of the team in football or soccer.
examples: The *fullback* blocked for the running back all game.
Both *fullbacks* got hurt in the second half.
He played *fullback* on his high school team.

gloss: The state of being full, especially the satisfied feeling after eating.
examples: Protein gives you a longer sense of *fullness*.
The *fullness* of the sound surprised me in that little room.
She felt an uncomfortable *fullness* after the second helping.

gloss: The killing of insects or pests by filling a space with poisonous gas.
examples: The house is closed for *fumigation* until Thursday.
*Fumigation* was the only thing that stopped the termites.
They warned the neighbors before the *fumigation*.

gloss: A basic rule or skill that everything else in a subject is built on.
examples: Coach spends the first week on *fundamentals*.
Patience is a *fundamental* of good teaching.
The course covers the *fundamentals* of accounting.
contrast: Usually plural: the *fundamentals*.

gloss: A style of dance music with a heavy beat and a strong bass line.
examples: The band plays *funk* and old soul covers.
You can hear the *funk* in that bass line.
He grew up on seventies *funk*.
contrast: *In a funk* is a separate meaning: in a low, gloomy mood.

gloss: A piece of furniture or a fitting that makes a room usable and comfortable.
examples: The apartment comes with basic *furnishings*.
They spent the whole budget on *furnishings*.
Every *furnishing* in the lobby was custom made.
contrast: Nearly always plural: home *furnishings*.

gloss: A sudden outburst of public anger about something.
examples: His comments caused a *furor* on social media.
The *furor* over the new logo lasted about a week.
The book stirred up a *furor* among historians.
contrast: An English *furor* is angry uproar, not a triumph like the Russian «фурор». The British spell it *furore*.

gloss: Unnecessary excitement or complaining about something small.
examples: Don't make a *fuss* — it's only a scratch.
What's all the *fuss* about?
She got her way without any *fuss*.

gloss: The quality of being pointless because nothing can be achieved.
examples: He finally saw the *futility* of arguing with her.
The report describes the *futility* of the whole operation.
There's a sense of *futility* in the office lately.

gloss: An increase in amount, value, or advantage.
examples: The fund posted a small *gain* last quarter.
Both parties made *gains* in the suburbs.
Any *gain* in speed costs you accuracy.

gloss: The way a person or animal walks.
examples: I recognized him by his rolling *gait*.
The therapist is working on her *gait* after surgery.
A horse has four natural *gaits*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *gate*.

gloss: An informal American word for a girl or woman.
examples: She's the *gal* who fixed my truck.
A couple of *gals* from work came along.
He's looking for a *gal* who likes fishing.
contrast: Casual and a little old-fashioned; in writing use *woman*.

gloss: Rude boldness; the nerve to do something shocking.
examples: He had the *gall* to ask for a raise that same week.
I can't believe the *gall* of these people.
She had the *gall* to show up uninvited.

gloss: The fastest running pace of a horse.
examples: The horse broke into a *gallop* across the field.
She rode at a full *gallop* down the beach.
The trainer gives him two easy *gallops* a week.

gloss: A small hard lump that forms in the gallbladder and can cause severe pain.
examples: The scan showed a large *gallstone*.
She had her gallbladder out because of *gallstones*.
A *gallstone* can block the duct and bring on an attack.

gloss: A clever opening move meant to gain an advantage, in chess or in a negotiation.
examples: His opening *gambit* was to offer half of what they asked.
The lawsuit was a *gambit* to delay the sale.
She's tried all the usual *gambits* to get out of chores.

gloss: A risky action taken in the hope of a good result.
examples: Quitting his job was a *gamble* that paid off.
Opening a restaurant is always a *gamble*.
They took a few *gambles* and lost most of them.

gloss: Someone who plays games of chance for money, especially often.
examples: Her father was a *gambler* who lost the house.
The casino watches its biggest *gamblers* closely.
He's a careful *gambler* who never bets the rent.

gloss: The activity of betting money on games or events.
examples: Online *gambling* is legal in some states.
*Gambling* cost him his savings.
The town depends on *gambling* for tax revenue.

gloss: A sex cell, such as an egg or a sperm, that joins with another to form a new organism.
examples: Each *gamete* carries half the usual number of chromosomes.
In humans the *gametes* are eggs and sperm.
The lab can freeze a *gamete* for years.

gloss: The third letter of the Greek alphabet, used in science to label a third kind of something.
examples: The symbol on the board is a lowercase *gamma*.
*Gamma* rays carry far more energy than X-rays.
He labeled the third curve with a *gamma*.

gloss: The whole range of something, from one extreme to the other.
examples: Her reaction ran the *gamut* from shock to laughter.
The menu covers the whole *gamut* of comfort food.
Prices run the *gamut* at that store.

gloss: The decay of body tissue that happens when blood stops reaching it.
examples: *Gangrene* set in and they had to amputate.
The wound got infected and turned to *gangrene*.
Diabetes raises the risk of *gangrene* in the feet.

gloss: A member of an organized group of violent criminals.
examples: The movie is about a young *gangster* in 1930s Chicago.
Two *gangsters* were arrested at the airport.
He dressed like a *gangster* for Halloween.

gloss: A bush with thick white flowers that smell very sweet.
examples: A single *gardenia* perfumed the whole room.
*Gardenias* need acidic soil and a lot of patience.
She wore a *gardenia* in her hair.

gloss: A deep red gemstone, the birthstone for January.
examples: Her ring has a small *garnet* in the center.
He collects *garnets* and other semiprecious stones.
The pendant is an antique *garnet* set in gold.
contrast: The stone is a *garnet*; the red fruit with the same name in Russian is a *pomegranate*.

gloss: A group of soldiers stationed in a town or fort, or the place where they stay.
examples: A small *garrison* held the fort all winter.
The army closed three *garrisons* last year.
News reached the *garrison* two days later.

gloss: A band worn around the leg to hold up a stocking.
examples: The bride wore a blue *garter* under her dress.
Old photographs show men wearing sock *garters*.
She keeps her grandmother's lace *garter* in a box.
contrast: A *garter snake* is a harmless striped snake, not a piece of clothing.

gloss: A lamp that burns gas, or the light such a lamp gives.
examples: The old street is still lit by *gaslights*.
They read by *gaslight* before the town had electricity.
A single *gaslight* flickered at the end of the alley.
contrast: Modern English also uses *gaslight* as a verb: to make someone doubt their own memory.

gloss: A quick, sharp breath taken in surprise, pain, or shock.
examples: A *gasp* went through the courtroom.
She let out a *gasp* when she saw the price.
There were *gasps* from the audience at the ending.

gloss: Someone who controls who or what is allowed through or in.
examples: His assistant is the *gatekeeper*, so be nice to her.
Editors used to be the *gatekeepers* of publishing.
Your family doctor acts as a *gatekeeper* to specialists.

gloss: An entrance, or something that leads on to something bigger.
examples: St. Louis calls itself the *gateway* to the West.
A stone *gateway* leads into the garden.
For some kids, vaping is a *gateway* to smoking.

gloss: A heavy protective glove that covers part of the arm.
examples: The knight's *gauntlet* was dented from the fight.
Welders wear leather *gauntlets*.
He pulled off one *gauntlet* to shake hands.
contrast: Two idioms: *throw down the gauntlet* (challenge someone) and *run the gauntlet* (face attacks from all sides).

gloss: A long, steady look at someone or something.
examples: She met his *gaze* without blinking.
His *gaze* drifted back to the window.
I felt their *gazes* on me as I walked in.

gloss: A newspaper, especially one that prints official announcements.
examples: The story ran in the local *gazette*.
He kept old *gazettes* from the 1940s in the attic.
Almost every county here has a *gazette* of some kind.
contrast: Mostly survives in newspaper names; the everyday word is *newspaper*.

gloss: A cold Spanish soup made from raw tomatoes, cucumber, and peppers.
examples: We had *gazpacho* on the patio.
Her *gazpacho* has too much garlic for me.
*Gazpacho* is perfect on a hot August day.

gloss: Someone with an intense, expert interest in a subject, especially computers.
examples: My roommate is a total computer *geek*.
The *geeks* in the IT room fixed it in a minute.
I'm a *geek* about old maps.
contrast: Once an insult, now usually friendly or even proud.

gloss: An old man, especially one seen as odd or grumpy.
examples: Some *geezer* yelled at us for parking there.
He calls himself an old *geezer* now.
A couple of *geezers* play chess in the park every morning.
contrast: In American English a *geezer* is an old man; in British slang it just means a guy.

gloss: A Japanese woman trained to entertain guests with music, dance, and conversation.
examples: A *geisha* poured the tea and began to play.
The book follows a young *geisha* in Kyoto.
Real *geishas* are rare today.

gloss: A clear substance made from animal bones that makes liquid set into a soft solid.
examples: Sprinkle the *gelatin* over cold water first.
Marshmallows are made with *gelatin*.
Vegetarians look for desserts without *gelatin*.
contrast: American *gelatin*, British *gelatine*.

gloss: A unit inside a cell that carries information passed from parents to children.
examples: Scientists identified the *gene* linked to the disease.
You get half your *genes* from each parent.
It's in his *genes* — his whole family is tall.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *jean*, as in a pair of jeans.

gloss: The study of family history, or a record of who descended from whom.
examples: She got into *genealogy* after a DNA test.
The library has *genealogies* of most local families.
Tracing his *genealogy* took him back to 1740.
contrast: Spelled -alogy, not -ology, though it sounds like the other -ology words.

gloss: A scientist who studies genes and how traits are inherited.
examples: A *geneticist* at the university explained the results.
*Geneticists* have mapped the whole human genome.
She trained as a *geneticist* before going into medicine.

gloss: A magical spirit in stories that appears from a lamp or bottle and grants wishes.
examples: If a *genie* gave you three wishes, what would you ask for?
The kids drew *genies* coming out of lamps.
That *genie* is out of the bottle now.

gloss: The complete set of genes in a living thing.
examples: The human *genome* was first mapped in 2003.
They sequenced the virus's *genome* in two days.
The *genomes* of related species overlap heavily.

gloss: A polite word for a man, or a man who behaves well toward others.
examples: A *gentleman* at the counter is asking for you.
Ladies and *gentlemen*, please take your seats.
He held the door for her — a real *gentleman*.
contrast: Irregular plural *gentlemen*; both forms end in the same -muhn sound.

gloss: A kind, careful way of treating people or things.
examples: He handled the puppy with surprising *gentleness*.
Her *gentleness* with the patients was obvious.
There was a *gentleness* in the way he said it.

gloss: A plain-looking rock that is hollow inside and lined with crystals.
examples: He cracked open a *geode* and found purple crystals.
The gift shop sells *geodes* by the pound.
A *geode* looks like an ordinary rock from the outside.

gloss: Someone who studies the earth's surface and how people live on it.
examples: A *geographer* from the state university mapped the flooding.
*Geographers* study cities as well as mountains.
She works as a *geographer* for the census bureau.

gloss: The way geography and national interests shape relations between countries.
examples: Oil pipelines are as much about *geopolitics* as engineering.
The course covers the *geopolitics* of the Arctic.
*Geopolitics* has pushed energy prices up again.
contrast: Ends in -s but takes a singular verb: *geopolitics* is complicated.

gloss: The branch of medicine that deals with the health of older people.
examples: She specialized in *geriatrics* after her residency.
*Geriatrics* is a growing field as the population ages.
The hospital opened a *geriatrics* clinic downtown.
contrast: Ends in -s but takes a singular verb, like *physics*.

gloss: A voting district drawn with unfair boundaries to help one political party win.
examples: Critics called the new map a blatant *gerrymander*.
The court threw out the district as an illegal *gerrymander*.
Both parties have drawn *gerrymanders* when they had the votes.
contrast: More often used as a verb (*to gerrymander*) or as *gerrymandering*.

gloss: Butter that has been melted and strained, used in Indian cooking.
examples: Fry the onions in *ghee* instead of oil.
*Ghee* keeps for months without refrigeration.
The store carries *ghee* in the international aisle.
contrast: The *gh* is a plain hard g: GEE.

gloss: A small cucumber pickled whole.
examples: The sandwich came with a *gherkin* on the side.
She chopped two *gherkins* into the potato salad.
A jar of *gherkins* costs three dollars.
contrast: The *gh* is a plain hard g: GUR-kin.

gloss: An evil spirit in stories that robs graves and eats the dead.
examples: The kids dressed as *ghouls* for Halloween.
A *ghoul* crawls out of the grave in the last scene.
The haunted house was full of plastic *ghouls*.
contrast: One syllable, GOOL — the h is silent.

gloss: An imaginary person of enormous size, or any unusually large person or company.
examples: The story is about a *giant* who lives above the clouds.
Two tech *giants* are fighting over the patent.
At six foot eight, he's a *giant* on the court.

gloss: Speech or writing that makes no sense at all.
examples: The contract is full of legal *gibberish*.
He was talking *gibberish* by the third hour.
To me that error message is pure *gibberish*.
contrast: Starts with a soft j sound: JIH-buh-rish.

gloss: A small ape with very long arms that swings through the trees of Southeast Asia.
examples: A *gibbon* swung across the enclosure in three moves.
*Gibbons* sing to mark their territory.
The zoo's new *gibbon* was born in April.
contrast: Hard g here (GIH-buhn), unlike *gibberish*.

gloss: One of the edible inner organs of a chicken or turkey, such as the heart or liver.
examples: Take the *giblets* out of the turkey before roasting.
She simmers the *giblets* to make gravy.
There's a bag of *giblets* tucked inside the bird.
contrast: Soft g (JIH-bluht), and almost always plural: *giblets*.

gloss: A unit of digital information equal to about one billion bits, used mainly to measure data speed.
examples: They're advertising *gigabit* internet in our neighborhood.
The connection tops out at two *gigabits* per second.
One *gigabit* is an eighth of a gigabyte.
contrast: A *gigabit* is eight times smaller than a gigabyte: speeds use bits, file sizes use bytes.

gloss: A unit of frequency equal to one billion cycles per second, used for processor and radio speeds.
examples: The laptop runs at three *gigahertz*.
Wi-Fi uses the 2.4 and 5 *gigahertz* bands.
One *gigahertz* used to be impressive.
contrast: The plural is the same word: five *gigahertz*, never gigahertzes.

gloss: A short, high laugh, often a nervous or silly one.
examples: A nervous *giggle* escaped before she could stop it.
The girls collapsed into *giggles*.
There was a *giggle* from the back of the class.

gloss: A sweet spiced cake or cookie flavored with ginger and molasses.
examples: The whole house smells like *gingerbread*.
We build a *gingerbread* house every Christmas.
She served warm *gingerbread* with whipped cream.

gloss: A hard, crisp cookie flavored with ginger.
examples: He dunked a *gingersnap* in his coffee.
A tin of *gingersnaps* sat by the register.
This *gingersnap* is too hard to bite.

gloss: An ancient Asian tree with fan-shaped leaves, often planted along city streets.
examples: The *ginkgo* on the corner turns bright yellow in November.
They planted *ginkgoes* all along the avenue.
She takes *ginkgo* for her memory.
contrast: Spelled g-i-n-k-g-o but said GING-koh.

gloss: The root of an Asian plant, taken as a medicine or tonic.
examples: He drinks *ginseng* tea every morning.
Wild *ginseng* sells for a fortune.
The label says the drink contains *ginseng*.

gloss: A woman or girl someone is romantically involved with.
examples: He brought his *girlfriend* to Thanksgiving.
His *girlfriend* is studying to be a nurse.
Both of my brothers brought their *girlfriends*.
contrast: American women also call their close female friends *girlfriends*; context decides.

gloss: A man in ancient Rome trained to fight others for public entertainment.
examples: A *gladiator* could win his freedom in the arena.
*Gladiators* fought with nets, swords, and tridents.
The museum has a helmet worn by a *gladiator*.

gloss: An exciting, attractive quality that makes something seem special and stylish.
examples: There's not much *glamor* in a twelve-hour shift.
The hotel has lost the *glamor* it had in the fifties.
She was drawn to the *glamor* of the fashion world.
contrast: Americans write *glamor* or *glamour*, but the adjective is always *glamorous*.

gloss: A quick look at someone or something.
examples: She gave the clock a quick *glance*.
They exchanged nervous *glances*.
At first *glance* the twins look identical.
